newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH FIRMS' EXPECTATIONS MORE BULLISH - SURVEY.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH FIRMS' EXPECTATIONS MORE BULLISH - SURVEY.

text.p: The Finnish corporate sector
took a clearly more bullish view of the future last October
than one year earlier, the Central Chamber of Commerce (KKK)
said in a statement on Tuesday.
A survey among 550 industrial and service sector companies
found that expectations for 1997 were clearly more upbeat than
the outlook for 1996 measured in an October 1995 survey.
The findings were presented in diffusion index form (the
percentage of respondents expecting an improvement minus those
expecting bleaker times):
Oct '96 survey Oct '95 survey
on '97 outlook on '96 outlook
Business cycle 47 34
Turnover 65 59
Domestic sales 52 43
Exports 64 54
Investment 15 18
Workforce 9 6
The survey was part of a survey of business climate in Europe conducted by chambers of commerce and coordinated by the Brussels-based Association of European Chambers of Commerce, Eurochambres.
A total of 97 regions in 12 Europan countries (Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, United Kingdom) were surveyed.
"Three EU counties show even higher expectations than last year: Finland, the United Kingdom and the Netherlands," it said, referring to turnover, domestic sales and exports prospects.
"In Finland, the service sector's positive expectations are the main contributors to the overall confident mood from entrepreneurs," it said.
"Total output (in Finland) will rise, spurred on by increases in both domestic and export sales," it said.

The unemployment outlook in Finland improved slightly since the previous survey in 1996, with service sector businesses expecting a stronger increase in labour while manufacturers see less expansion of their workforces, it said.
After two years of strong growth in investments, Finnish entrepreneurs expect more modest investment growth in 1997, Eurochambers said.
Efforts of governments to meet the criteria of the Maastrict treaty would affect European business in both positive and negative ways, it said.

"Budgetary cuts suppress domestid demand, but on the other hand, the resulting better-balanced national budgets instil faith in the financial markets, thereby lowering interest rates," Eurochambers said.
